messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 58
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Product Manager
  trauma_type: Torture
  pcl5: 55

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Auditory (Language Confusion): Incomprehensible chatter, Somatic (Dizziness): Feeling dizzy or lightheaded, Auditory (Sirens): Sirens
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Stressors: avoid anything that could be stressful, Body Monitoring: constantly check body for signs of danger or injury, Avoid Uniform or Weapons: Military, police uniforms or weapons
  Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
  Negative Appraisals: Mistrust: People can't be trusted, Intrinsic Fault: There is something about me that made the event happen, No Good Ahead: Nothing good can happen to me anymore

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Ravi Patel, a 58-year-old product manager, came to treatment after years of trying to contain the aftereffects of being detained and tortured while visiting extended family abroad. He described being held in a cramped concrete room where men shouted over one another in a language he could not fully understand, their words fast and jagged, impossible to follow and therefore impossible to predict. At several points he was struck, shoved, and forced to stand when he was already faint; what stayed with him most was the combination of dizziness, the panic of not knowing what was being said around him, and the sudden blare of sirens outside that he came to hear as a sign that something worse was about to happen. He survived and returned to the United States, but he had come back with a conviction that people could not be trusted, that there was something about him that had made him a target, and that whatever future he had imagined for himself had ended there.

In the months afterward, those beliefs settled into the way he organized his life. Because he was certain the world was fundamentally unsafe and that he himself was somehow marked for harm, Ravi began avoiding anything that felt remotely stressful. At work, where he had once been known for leading tense product meetings and navigating conflict between engineering and sales, he now delegated high-stakes presentations and delayed difficult conversations if he could. He also went out of his way to avoid police officers, security guards, and anyone carrying a visible weapon; if he saw a uniform in the lobby of his office building, he would wait outside or circle the block until the person was gone. The more he arranged his days around reducing risk, the more his life seemed shrunken and joyless to him, which only confirmed his sense that nothing good was ahead and that he was no longer the man he had been.

His beliefs also kept his body in a state of readiness that he could not switch off. Ravi said that even in his own house, with his wife asleep beside him, he could not relax in any settled way. He woke repeatedly in the night and checked doors, windows, and the hallway outside the bedroom, feeling briefly foolish but more afraid of what would happen if he stopped checking. When someone touched him unexpectedly—a colleague brushing past him in a conference room, his wife placing a hand on his shoulder from behind—his whole body jolted before he knew where he was. He understood intellectually that he was home and not imprisoned, yet he had come to believe danger could appear without warning and that trusting apparent safety was exactly how people got hurt.

That constant alarm made ordinary sensations and sounds feel loaded. Because he was so vigilant, any lightheadedness during the day—a skipped lunch, standing up too quickly after hours at his desk—immediately caught his attention and felt like the beginning of the same bodily collapse he had experienced during captivity. He monitored himself closely for signs of injury or danger, checking whether his heart was racing, whether his balance was off, whether something in his body was warning him that he had missed a threat. The more he scanned, the more often he noticed dizziness. A distant siren while he was driving to the office could pull him out of the present in seconds, and overhearing rapid conversation in a language he did not understand in the cafeteria or on the train made his chest tighten before he could tell himself that these were just coworkers or strangers minding their own business.

Over time, his efforts to protect himself fed the very experiences he feared. Avoiding stressful situations left him with fewer chances to discover that he could tolerate tension without catastrophe, and his shrinking world began to look like evidence that the future really was closed off. His body monitoring made every minor sensation feel significant, so dizziness showed up more often in his awareness and became a cue for danger rather than a passing physical state. Avoiding uniforms also kept them charged; seeing a police officer near his office entrance did not become routine, it remained an event he had to organize himself around. At home, his wife had grown frustrated and saddened by how he pulled away from restaurants, crowds, and even family gatherings if there might be loud noise or confusion. Ravi interpreted this distance as further proof that he was damaged and that closeness with others was no longer safe or possible.

What finally brought him in was an incident at work. During a cross-functional meeting, two visitors were speaking rapidly to each other in a language he did not understand when a siren sounded outside the building. A coworker touched his arm to ask if he was all right, and he recoiled so sharply that the room went silent. He left the office, sat in his car feeling dizzy and ashamed, and could not make himself go back inside. He told the therapist he was frightened that his life was narrowing to the point where work, marriage, and sleep would all be governed by the same fear. At the same time, he said he still hoped for some way to believe that not every sound, sensation, or person meant danger, and that he might one day be able to rest without checking whether he was safe.
